posts.note: 95-word podcast blurb about PBM leaders correcting the congressional record; no forward-looking claims.
Personal essay in memoriam Jake Seliger; only truisms ('we're gonna die'), nothing forecast-like.
Review of two JAMA papers on ADHD medication, cardiovascular risk and mortality. One borderline risk summary logged with forward_looking false. Fermata/Monarch eTNS mention is present tense.

Acadia Healthcare / NY Times essay on locked units. Two forecasts (doubt on prosecution; litigation will ensue) plus one borderline efficacy claim with forward_looking false. 'There should be vastly more of these' is normative and not logged.
Part one of a Mark Horowitz interview; interviewee statements are not the author's. One trivial next-installment promise logged.
Part two of the Horowitz interview; no author forecasts. 'Keep following my interview' is an imperative, not logged.
Part three of the Horowitz interview; author's remarks are present-tense analysis (drugs causing vs. not solving problems), no forecasts.
Guest column by Joanna Strober (Midi Health) on the DEA telemedicine proposal, hosted and endorsed by the author. Two guest forecasts logged with own_claim false.
Essay on repeated blast exposure in special operations warriors after a Homebase visit; normative calls ('it's our job to fund') and no forecasts.

Essay to VC/PE investors; illustrative funnel math the author calls not serious. Brain stimulation as the future, retirement extrapolation, the 2.5-physician estimate, the payment-infrastructure call, and a borderline intent declaration logged.

statements.quote: Yes, your ADHD medication might kill you. But, it’s more likely your ADHD will kill you on it’s own if left untreated.
statements.context: Summary paragraph of a review of two JAMA papers (Zhang et al. 2023 JAMA Psychiatry on ADHD medication and long-term cardiovascular risk; Li et al. 2024 JAMA on ADHD pharmacotherapy and mortality). The author concludes that ADHD medication raises cardiovascular risk a little (mainly hypertension and arterial disease), but untreated ADHD carries a higher and earlier risk of death.
statements.note: Borderline: general risk summary of published data, not a prediction of a future event. Logged for recall with forward_looking false.

statements.quote: I also have every reason to doubt this will be the case.
statements.context: Reacting to the NY Times investigation alleging Acadia Healthcare held psychiatric patients against their will for insurance money. In the preceding paragraph the author hopes the described circumstances will be investigated and, if substantiated, every person involved will face criminal charges and prosecution; 'this' refers to that hope. He then says he doubts it will happen.
statements.note: Negative call: the author doubts the Acadia allegations will be investigated and prosecuted (legal enforcement). Antecedent is in the prior paragraph.

statements.quote: It is a profitable for-profit company. At least, it was profitable prior to the litigation that will now ensue.
statements.context: About Acadia Healthcare, the publicly traded psychiatric hospital operator accused in the NY Times of holding patients against their will. The author shows its recent financials and asserts that litigation will now follow the Times report, implying its profitability is at risk.
statements.note: Compound: litigation against Acadia will ensue (explicit); its profitability held only before that litigation (implied).

statements.quote: Locked units? No! The data says it’s between implausible and impossible that current treatment will help.
statements.context: Closing argument that insurers should not pay for locked inpatient psychiatric units. The author cites open-door studies (Norway RCT, German 15-year observational study) and antidepressant onset-of-action data to argue that short locked stays with medication as the mainstay cannot plausibly help patients.
statements.note: Borderline: efficacy judgment about current locked-unit treatment, not a dated prediction. Logged for recall with forward_looking false.

statements.quote: Thanks for joining us for part one of this interview! Stay tuned for more.
statements.context: Close of part one of a three-part interview with Dr. Mark Horowitz (co-founder of Outro Health, author of the Maudsley Deprescribing Guidelines) on antidepressant withdrawal. The author promises further installments in The Frontier Psychiatrists.
statements.note: Trivial: promise of further interview parts (own newsletter). Logged for recall only.

statements.quote: A new proposal from the Drug Enforcement Agency threatens to limit the ability to prescribe controlled substances via telemedicine. If finalized, it would severely hurt the telehealth industry that took off during the pandemic, but more importantly, it would hurt women.
statements.context: Guest column by Joanna Strober, founder of Midi Health (virtual midlife care for over 100K women), introduced and endorsed by the author as a call to action to the DEA. She states that a proposed DEA rule on telemedicine prescribing of controlled substances, if finalized, would severely hurt the telehealth industry and women who rely on medications such as Ativan, Lunesta, gabapentin and Suboxone.
statements.note: Guest's words, not the author's. The author hosts the piece and endorses the cause ('what kinds of care are on the line', 'this crucial issue') without restating the forecast.

statements.quote: Gabapentin, which is crucial for managing hot flashes and sleep issues, especially for breast cancer survivors who can’t take hormonal treatments, would be affected. As would Suboxone, which is used to treat opioid dependence
statements.context: Same guest column by Joanna Strober (Midi Health). Conditional on the DEA telemedicine proposal being finalized, she lists medications whose telehealth prescribing would be affected: anxiolytics and sleep aids (Ativan, Lunesta), gabapentin, and Suboxone for opioid dependence.
statements.note: Guest's words. Scope claim about which drugs the proposed DEA rule would cover; conditional on finalization.

statements.quote: I often explain that I think brain stimulation is the future of psychiatric care, given remission of depression rapidly has been demonstrated repeatedly and at large scale.
statements.context: Opening of an essay aimed at venture capital and private equity investors who ask 'Why isn't someone already doing this?'. The author, an interventional psychiatrist, restates his standing view that brain stimulation (TMS and related neuromodulation) will be the future of psychiatric care, citing large real-world TMS datasets and Stanford accelerated TMS in footnote 1.
statements.note: Restatement of a recurring call ('I often explain'). No date.

statements.quote: Many now don't want any part of what you have to offer. We don't like you. We don't trust you. And we won’t have anything to do with you.
statements.context: Addressed to venture and private equity investors. The author says their record of funding bad mental-health ideas (he cites Done) has shrunk the pool of clinicians who can build better care models and are willing to work with them; the group he speaks for will refuse to work with such investors.
statements.note: Borderline: declaration of intent on behalf of a group of clinicians rather than a resolvable forecast. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: May docs are going to stop practicing soon: Nearly 30% of physicians retire between 60 and 65 years old, and 12% retire before 60
statements.context: Step in an illustrative back-of-envelope count of how many US psychiatrists could lead tech-enabled, value-based mental health companies. From about 331 candidates the author removes those who will retire soon, citing AMA Insurance Agency survey data, leaving about 200. 'May' is a typo for 'Many' in the original.
statements.note: Demographic extrapolation inside a calculation the author calls 'not a serious article when it comes to math'.

statements.quote: Now we are at 25 companies founded or hiring CMOs from 25 physicians. 90% of startups fail: that is 2.5 physicians left winning the race to become a billion dollar company (at a minimum).
statements.context: End of the illustrative funnel: from 56,536 US psychiatrists, through TMS and ketamine practitioners, research authorship, in-network status, retirement, Y Combinator acceptance and startup failure rates, the author estimates that roughly 2.5 physician-led companies could become billion-dollar companies. He states up front that the math is not serious and he is making a point.
statements.note: Illustrative numeric estimate; author says 'It's not a serious article when it comes to math—I'm making a point.' The number is rhetorical; the direction (very few) is sincere.

statements.quote: Because accepting the current payment infrastructure means building less profitable businesses, and that won’t win for patients.
statements.context: Conclusion of the essay. The author answers 'Why isn't anyone doing this?' by arguing that care-delivery companies built on the current payment infrastructure will be less profitable than insurers or pharma (he cites UnitedHealth Group's 540 billion market cap) and will not deliver wins for patients; new contract, risk and financial models are needed.
statements.note: Conditional/general call: accepting the current payment infrastructure implies less profitable businesses that do not win for patients.
